Death in the Chicken House

By: Joy Summers | Commission

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
The implosion at Daybreak farms as greed, corruption and mismanagement takes its toll

Unique Selling Point:
Excellent sources and access and NSPCA footage - an unfolding story in courts, not about a chicken farm but about ongoing state capture in the chicken business

Summary:
Summary:
Starving chickens eating each other in horrific conditions as the NSPCA inspectors swooped on Daybreak farms to cull over 200 000 chickens; unpaid workers burning maize and protesting at the gates; a board chair forcing through over R600 000 payment in board fees and then fleeing the coup as Daybreak – a massive integrated chicken business wholly owned by the PIC, the Competition Commission and the UIF, implodes


Further information:
More information
Is this the end of Daybreak as it lurches from one crisis to the next? It’s a company that has 7% of the market, slaughters 6million chickens every 42 days, and employs over 3000 workers. In 2016 the PIC bought it for R1.2 billion rand, paid well connected businessman Kholofelo Maponya millions in fees for bringing the deal to the table and handed him the position of CEO. Within 6 months the company was insolvent, and the PIC removed him. But what did it matter – with two transactions close to R1.8 billion rand for his company and fees for each amounting to a total of around R60 million, he just walked away, leaving the PIC to pick up the pieces and take ownership of the company. Later at the Mpati commission they conceded that a single entity company should not be able to access that kind of business from the PIC.

After Maponya, the PIC put in their own people who brought in one of SA’s top chicken experts. For the next couple of years, the company began to turn around and even showed profits. But their success was a poisoned chalice. The PIC saw a gap and wanted to sell the business. That brought in every grasping venal faction who wanted a piece of the action and a shareholding. The PIC company secretary who remains in her position supported a board that was illegally constituted and began a looting spree of note. R200 million to a connected law firm who was later ordered to pay back the money, motorcars, R50 million to a branding company owned by Cedric Mamabolo…R80 000 for a four paragraph Christmas message from the board chair to staff and bloated management structures. A google search on 3 critical board members shows a tainted history in other government sectors. We will go into these.

But as the looting progressed the business ran into trouble. Whistleblowers were hounded out and harassed, the former CEO was terminated and later won his case at the CCMA. Daybreak was making headlines, and a server with critical financial information was stolen after the company made the news.

The Hawks came in and did nothing, but the real inaction came from the PIC who could have saved this company at every turn. At the heart of it, is the company secretary of the PIC who remains in her position despite bringing in board members who actively looted the company.

“They should all be charged!” bemoans one source, the companies act is clear. But the PIC and our criminal justice system do absolutely nothing.


The PIC commissioned several forensic reports, kept them private, and then took no action. At least five boards have come and gone and on Friday 16th May the PIC put in a new board into Daybreak. But its likely too late. An internal source that is now part of that board told Carte Blanche that to save the company they will need another billion rand. The PIC have reluctantly put in R250 million, but those funds are already allocated.

The NSPCA have won its case to stop all farming and slaughtering for now. So, despite appearances it may be the end of the road for Daybreak. And what an irony it would be if the UIF, a 33.3% shareholder puts another 3300 workers on the streets.

Liquidation Application
on Tuesday this week, fed up farmers who have contracts to grow Daybreak chickens are going to court to put it into liquidation. They are owed R20 million rand. There are 38 contract growers- some have found other markets; others have mothballed their farms, and the workers have already lost their jobs. In fact, it was the farmers who first alerted the NSPCA to the terrible animal abuse as Daybreak left thousands of chickens to starve to death.

This story raises so many questions, but one thing is clear, an asset manager like the PIC should never be running a chicken farm. It has failed dismally. It’s a clear-cut case of greed, corruption and mismanagement says a former CEO.

Carte Blanche investigates.

DEATH IN THE CHICKEN HOUSE FINAL SCRIPT
FACT CHECKED :SCRIPT FOR MIHLE

VO 1
You can't hide the stench of sustained corruption forever

In late April, these shocking visuals became a symbol of how Daybreak executives had been running this huge poultry business in Mpumalanga and Limpopo

Nazareth Appalsamy Senior Inspector: NSPCA
Birds were cannibalizing each other and there was no food.

VO2
The NSPCA had a front row seat on this horror show, that sparked national outrage.

Nazareth Appalsamy
We found birds with large open wounds and other birds being eaten alive.

VO3
Daybreak breeds, raises and slaughters chickens for sale to the public: a million and a half birds a week at full production

But it's become an embarrassment to its owners - the Public Investment Corporation or PIC.

Sabelo
So it was a mess for the PIC, But I think it was also a case of the chickens coming home to roost. They had built this monster.

VO 4
The PIC, a 100% state-owned company, manages about R3 trillion rand in assets for government employees yet apparently can’t ensure a chicken business it owns, is run properly.

Five years ago, a former employee blew the whistle on the looting she witnessed, but she was charged with defamation, gagged, fired, and later arrested.

Sabelo
The very same people that at some point you were lauding as the superstar black management, that was giving you the blueprint of how to do empowerment properly, but they then become the first victims, when the corruption wolf comes knocking on the door.

VO 5
It appears Daybreak has been a problem child for the PIC for some time, but its executives claim numerous interventions haven’t produced the desired results.

It’s a breathtaking understatement, showing a complete lack of accountability in the face of Daybreak’s destruction.

FADE TO BLACK

VO 6
To understand Daybreak’s demise, we went back ten years, and looked at some of the personalities who’ve had a hand in running it.

Meet Kholofelo Maponya, the man who was loaned over a billion rand by the PIC to buy the business. In 2015 Daybreak was already in financial distress.

The official line is that the deal was done to “further transformation in agriculture, support food security and job creation, and address poverty in rural communities.”

Lourensa
It's just difficult for me to try to understand why you would want to buy a company that is so deeply in trouble.
Maponya:
We bought a lemon to make lemonade.
Lourensa:
Were you able to make any lemonade?
Maponya
Yes, we were on our way, but we were hindered from day one. It is still possible to make lemonade out of it. The only problem is that you have a partner, or you have a financier who doesn't know how to make lemonade and who insists on being in the driver's seat.

LINK
Maponya did very well out of Daybreak. He convinced the PIC to pay R1.2 billion rand for the company. That earned him millions in fees and a healthy salary. Pity then, that less than a year later, the company was technically bankrupt.

VO 7
But Maponya has little good to say about the PIC.

Maponya
Our experience with the PIC was not one of mismanagement. It was actually one of betrayal.
VO 8
Maponya says the PIC withheld R100 million of working capital, and removed guarantees, and that he invested the R11 million-rand fee he was paid for completing the transaction, back into the business.

The PIC denies this, saying bad decisions made by the management under Maponya were responsible for the company's troubles.

Lourensa:
What about reports about the salary that you paid yourself?
Maponya
I didn't pay myself a salary.

VO 9
A lot has been written about Maponya. He is the son of a well-known businessman and he lives large. He has an astonishing hundred companies under his name, and flies around in a R14 million king air. He denies buying the plane with Daybreak money.

Maponya:
The Daybreak transaction was cash negative. It would have been a miracle to buy a plane out of it.
Lourensa: What did you take home after that deal?
Maponya: Nothing.
Lourensa: Nothing?
Maponya:
Nothing! We did not take home any money. We actually left the money that was part of the money we spent in the business.

VO 10
Investigative journalist Sabelo Skiti has long followed the Daybreak story.

Sabelo Skiti
I like to call these types of individuals the fortunate businessmen in South Africa, he is a gentleman that is very well known to the PIC and is probably the only person who is smiling as a result of the Daybreak deal.

VO11
Maponya left Daybreak about 18 months later. The business was now over R500 million in debt.

But he blames shadowy influences rather than his own management.

Sabelo
History will tell us that the PIC has been one of those institutions that has been targeted by people that are politically linked to politicians.

VO 12
The Mpati Commission, set up in 2018 to investigate corruption at the PIC, flagged the exorbitant amount of money loaned to Maponya’s company MMI -in two separate deals. Daybreak was just one of them. The commission made no findings against him

Lourensa:
And do you think that you were sort of worked out because you were not politically connected?
Maponya:
Yes. No, I don't think so, I know.

VO 13
By 2018, the PIC had poured close to R2 billion into Daybreak - sourced from the Unemployment Insurance Fund and government pensions. To this day, Daybreak still owes more than R250 million to its creditors.

Jannie Oosthuizen: Chief Negotiator PSA
How many times more must we raise a concern? How many times more must we refer you to your own rules. Because we see the writing is on the wall.

VO 14
Jannie Oosthuizen, Chief negotiator at the Public Service Association, a registered union, says the PIC is betraying government employees.

Jannie Oosthuizen
We do not think that the PIC has the capacity as an investment agent to invest in unlisted companies. It is proven over and over again that the unlisted companies that they have invested in, uh, goes under.

VO 15
To fix Daybreak after Maponya’s departure, the PIC brought in this man, Boas Seruwe. Under him, the chicken business finally began showing signs of settling.

LINK
By 2017 the new CEO and a small Daybreak team began to turn the company around, even turning a profit. But their success would be short-lived, because the profits brought in the vultures.

V0 16
In 2020 the PIC installed a new board at Daybreak chaired by this man, Lerato Nage.

Sabelo Skiti
A basic Google search will show you that this is a gentleman who's well versed in arriving at state owned entities, and pretty much soon after he arrives, these things fall into chaos.

VO 17
This is the board that would ultimately break the company. Recorded emails show Boas Seruwe, by then around 3 years at the helm of the company, was told to appoint specific service providers and pay them millions. He refused.

Sabelo Skiti
And you are seeing the chairperson write to the CEO. in what is astonishing, copying the service provider and virtually instructing the CEO that, um, the service provider is unhappy with the price. Please give him the price that he demands.

VO 18
Nage denies this, saying he had no involvement in procurement.

The paper trail shows an apparent feeding frenzy

Link
A single law firm charged over R100 million rand in legal fees, and this forensic report shows pages of clearly fictitious invoices
In one instance one of the lawyers claims to have worked for 34 hours in a single day

Lourensa
Why do you think the PIC seemingly did nothing to prevent this looting?
Jannie Oosthuizen
Well, we are of the view that there might be political influence. That is the only conclusion that we can draw /why did you allow this to continue going on and keep on pumping money into that? And you don't get a return on investment.

V0 19
At the centre of much of this alleged wrongdoing is another of the past decade’s cast of characters: the PIC Company Secretary, Bongani Mathebula. Tasked with advising on corporate governance, among other things, it’s alleged she had the power to manipulate who got onto the Daybreak board.

Sabelo Skiti
I think she certainly played the key role for me.

VO 20
Several sources point to Mathebula as a former associate of the law firm that allegedly looted millions from Daybreak. She denies this and says she knew nothing of the payments to the firm.

Sabelo
Remember, when you've got outside interests, whether it's politicians or people with political power, um, wanting to take over a state institution, you still need/ enablers.

V0 21
Mathebula says that as PIC company secretary, she’s not party to or responsible for Daybreak’s operational activities or its demise, adding that board appointments are approved by the PIC. She denies being corrupt, an enabler of corruption, or politically affiliated.

VO 22
But Maponya suspects Bongani Mathebula played a role in misappropriating his Daybreak shares.
Lourensa:
So, the PIC never bought back your shares?
Maponya:
No. They illegally took my shares. So, when we do every transaction, we have empty or blank transfer forms signed at the company secretary's office. So, they went to the company secretary's office, and they signed over my shares to themselves. I never signed the shares.
Lourensa:
That's astonishing.
Maponya
Can you believe it? I still can't. Ten years on.

VO 23
Mathebula says anyone with evidence of theft should provide proof.

LINK
So, the Daybreak millions were looted, the forensic reports piled up, at least one whistleblower sounded the alarm, and yet the PIC just looked the other way, again and again and again.

VO 24
In its response, the PIC says it is not responsible for the operations and finances of Daybreak: that responsibility lies with the board and management.
The PIC provides funding and nominates directors in investee companies, but “does not guarantee and does not sanction their conduct”.
It says it has conducted forensic investigations following several whistleblower reports, has implemented their recommendations, and will continue to do so.
Admitting previous interventions have not yielded the desired results, the PIC says it won’t abandon the investment as this would automatically mean its demise.
Staff protesting up sound
VO 25
It's clear from these responses that neither the PIC nor its former executives believe they should be held to account. But worse was to come: In May - Daybreak completely unraveled and interim board chair, Bojane Segooa, wasn't about to hang around

Up sound Staff
You know its very painful to hear icompany is down the drain but the management are still getting their 50%

LINK
Imagine the scene here just a few weeks ago, staff were protesting because they hadn’t been paid, and the NSPCA were coming across horrific scenes of animal abuse inside the company, and amidst this crisis, what did the chairperson do? She demanded her board fees of more than R600 000 and then she cut and ran. …exemplary corporate governance.

VO 25A
At the time, Daybreak had just 2 million in the bank.

Segooa, responded:
She did not force through any board payments. She was owed board fees when she resigned, which she has since forfeited.

She adds that she acted in Daybreak’s best interests, that the company was “fully functional” when she resigned, and workers’ salaries were paid on time.

But we’ve confirmed that she did receive almost R625 000 before she resigned

Pause

The NSPCA’s Nazareth Appalsamy, found anything BUT a fully functional company when he arrived at Daybreak late in April

Naz Appalsamy Senior Inspector, NSPCA
At first we were we were met with horror and then it turned to anger because basically through negligence, these birds have suffered unnecessarily

VO 26
After laying criminal charges against Daybreak, the NSPCA won its case against the company, and a court ordered that the operation be shut down.

Naz
We held daybreak solely responsible. At first there was cooperation, but when they learned through the media that the board was going to be criminally held liable, we did not get much assistance thereafter.

VO 27
Daybreak made it clear that we could expect no comment but referred us to a media statement announcing that it had been put into voluntary business rescue to save 2 800 jobs. It’s a decision supported by the PIC

But until the NSPCA court order is lifted, business can’t resume at Daybreak. There is almost nothing left to plunder… and the fate of the employees now hangs in the balance.

It’s a company that has 7% of the market, slaughters 6million chickens every 42 days, and employs over 3000 workers. In 2016 the PIC bought it for R1.2 billion rand, paid well connected businessman Kholofelo Maponya millions in fees for bringing the deal to the table and handed him the position of CEO. Within 6 months the company was insolvent, and the PIC removed him. But what did it matter – with two transactions close to R1.8 billion rand for his company and fees for each amounting to a total of around R60 million, he just walked away, leaving the PIC to pick up the pieces and take ownership of the company. The PIC company secretary who remains in her position supported a board that was illegally constituted and began a looting spree of note. R200 million to a connected law firm who was later ordered to pay back the money, motorcars, R50 million to a branding company owned by Cedric Mamabolo…R80 000 for a four paragraph Christmas message from the board chair to staff and bloated management structures. Whistleblowers were hounded out and harassed, the former CEO was terminated and later won his case at the CCMA. Daybreak was making headlines, and a server with critical financial information was stolen after the company made the news. The Hawks came in and did nothing, but the real inaction came from the PIC who could have saved this company at every turn. At least five boards have come and gone and on Friday 16th May the PIC put in a new board into Daybreak. But its likely too late. An internal source that is now part of that board told Carte Blanche that to save the company they will need another billion rand. The PIC have reluctantly put in R250 million, but those funds are already allocated. The NSPCA have won its case to stop all farming and slaughtering for now. In fact, it was the farmers who first alerted the NSPCA to the terrible animal abuse as Daybreak left thousands of chickens to starve to death. This story raises so many questions, but one thing is clear, an asset manager like the PIC should never be running a chicken farm. It has failed dismally. metadata.Summary: Summary: Starving chickens eating each other in horrific conditions as the NSPCA inspectors swooped on Daybreak farms to cull over 200 000 chickens; unpaid workers burning maize and protesting at the gates; a board chair forcing through over R600 000 payment in board fees and then fleeing the coup as Daybreak – a massive integrated chicken business wholly owned by the PIC, the Competition Commission and the UIF, implodes
metadata.Further information: More information Is this the end of Daybreak as it lurches from one crisis to the next? It’s a company that has 7% of the market, slaughters 6million chickens every 42 days, and employs over 3000 workers. In 2016 the PIC bought it for R1.2 billion rand, paid well connected businessman Kholofelo Maponya millions in fees for bringing the deal to the table and handed him the position of CEO. Within 6 months the company was insolvent, and the PIC removed him. But what did it matter – with two transactions close to R1.8 billion rand for his company and fees for each amounting to a total of around R60 million, he just walked away, leaving the PIC to pick up the pieces and take ownership of the company. Later at the Mpati commission they conceded that a single entity company should not be able to access that kind of business from the PIC. After Maponya, the PIC put in their own people who brought in one of SA’s top chicken experts. For the next couple of years, the company began to turn around and even showed profits. But their success was a poisoned chalice. The PIC saw a gap and wanted to sell the business. That brought in every grasping venal faction who wanted a piece of the action and a shareholding. The PIC company secretary who remains in her position supported a board that was illegally constituted and began a looting spree of note. R200 million to a connected law firm who was later ordered to pay back the money, motorcars, R50 million to a branding company owned by Cedric Mamabolo…R80 000 for a four paragraph Christmas message from the board chair to staff and bloated management structures. A google search on 3 critical board members shows a tainted history in other government sectors. We will go into these. But as the looting progressed the business ran into trouble. Whistleblowers were hounded out and harassed, the former CEO was terminated and later won his case at the CCMA. Daybreak was making headlines, and a server with critical financial information was stolen after the company made the news. The Hawks came in and did nothing, but the real inaction came from the PIC who could have saved this company at every turn. At the heart of it, is the company secretary of the PIC who remains in her position despite bringing in board members who actively looted the company. “They should all be charged!” bemoans one source, the companies act is clear. But the PIC and our criminal justice system do absolutely nothing. The PIC commissioned several forensic reports, kept them private, and then took no action. At least five boards have come and gone and on Friday 16th May the PIC put in a new board into Daybreak. But its likely too late. An internal source that is now part of that board told Carte Blanche that to save the company they will need another billion rand. The PIC have reluctantly put in R250 million, but those funds are already allocated. The NSPCA have won its case to stop all farming and slaughtering for now. So, despite appearances it may be the end of the road for Daybreak. And what an irony it would be if the UIF, a 33.3% shareholder puts another 3300 workers on the streets. Liquidation Application on Tuesday this week, fed up farmers who have contracts to grow Daybreak chickens are going to court to put it into liquidation. They are owed R20 million rand. There are 38 contract growers- some have found other markets; others have mothballed their farms, and the workers have already lost their jobs. In fact, it was the farmers who first alerted the NSPCA to the terrible animal abuse as Daybreak left thousands of chickens to starve to death. This story raises so many questions, but one thing is clear, an asset manager like the PIC should never be running a chicken farm. It has failed dismally. It’s a clear-cut case of greed, corruption and mismanagement says a former CEO. Carte Blanche investigates.
